text: Key-based authentication is the foundation, not the finish line. sshd_config has several other settings worth hardening, each closing a gap keys alone don't touch. Every change here needs the same habit first: sshd -t checks the config's syntax without restarting the service, catching a typo before it breaks every future SSH connection to the box instead of after.

PermitRootLogin no means an administrator must log in as a named user and sudo to root, instead of logging in as root directly — leaving a record of which account performed the privileged action. Changing the port away from 22 isn't real security on its own, since a determined attacker can still scan for an open SSH service, but it cuts the automated scanning noise that hits port 22 nonstop.

AllowUsers names exactly which accounts may authenticate over SSH at all, even if others exist with valid keys. DenyUsers does the opposite, blocking specific accounts while leaving everyone else alone. Both are checked after standard authentication, so they're a hard backstop — a denied user is rejected even with a perfectly valid key. On an SELinux host, a changed port also needs its own semanage rule to bind correctly.

Disabling password authentication entirely is the step most likely to lock you out if done carelessly. The safe order: confirm key login already works from a second, still-open session, run sshd -t, restart sshd, and only then close the original session after a brand-new connection succeeds with keys alone. Skipping that second session is the single most common way administrators strand themselves outside their own server.

Put it together and SSH goes from key-protected to genuinely hardened: no direct root, a quieter port, a named allow-list, and no password fallback at all. Next up: fail2ban, which watches for failed login attempts and bans the source IP automatically — useful defense in depth even after every one of these settings is already in place.
